The White-chinned Woodcreeper Dendrocincla merula is a medium-sized furnariid that forages along vertical trunks in the understory of lowland Amazonian forests. The species exhibits pronounced sexual size dimorphism, with adult females attaining an asymptotic body mass of approximately 49.5 grams [Wwi = approximately 49.5 grams], whereas males typically reach a larger stable adult weight of 57 grams [Wwi = 57 grams]. This difference likely reflects the demands of different foraging niches or possibly the energetic costs of nest defense. Hatchlings emerge from the egg at a far more modest size; the initial wet weight of a neonate is estimated at approximately 5 grams [Ww0 = approximately 5 grams]. This represents a considerable relative investment by the female given her own mass. The developmental trajectory from hatchling to independence is rapid by suboscine standards, with the fledgling stage occurring just 24 days after hatching [tx = 24 days after hatching] under the active thermal conditions typical of this species, with body temperatures around 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. The brief nestling period demands high rates of parental provisioning to support such swift somatic growth.

Reproductive output in Dendrocincla merula appears to be constrained by the short breeding window of the wet season. Breeding females typically produce a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch], a value consistent with the small clutch size typical of many cavity-nesting woodcreepers. However, the maximum clutch frequency in a given season is approximately 2 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 2 clutches per year], allowing for replacement of failed attempts or, rarely, a second successful brood. The maximum daily reproduction rate is thus approximately 2 offspring per year [Ri = approximately 2 offspring per year] at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. The limited annual reproductive output is balanced by a comparatively long-lived adult stage. The maximum recorded lifespan for this species, extrapolated from field recapture data, is approximately 10.5 years [am = approximately 10.5 years] under wild conditions at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], an age which allows multiple breeding seasons over a lifetime.

The age at which neonates emerge from the egg is somewhat protracted relative to the rapid fledging period. Incubation lasts for 23 days [ab = 23 days], a duration that is considerably longer than the 24-day nestling phase the chick will experience after hatching at a temperature of 31 °C [T = 31 °C]. Interestingly, this incubation period is documented at a lower average nest temperature of 31 °C [T = 31 °C], reflecting the fact that brooding adults do not always maintain full contact with the clutch during foraging bouts or that ambient nest cavity temperatures are lower than core body temperature. At this cooler incubation environment, the embryo develops slowly but steadily, relying on the substantial yolk reserves of the initial wet mass of 5 grams [Ww0 = 5 grams]. The sharp contrast between the 31 °C incubation environment and the 40.2 °C at which active chicks and adults operate underscores the energetic transition that occurs at the moment of hatching.

The attainment of sexual maturity in Dendrocincla merula occurs well after the fledgling has reached nutritional independence. Puberty, defined as the development of functional gonads, is typically reached at 72 days after hatching [tp = 72 days after hatching] when individuals are maintained at a body temperature of approximately 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This corresponds to the post-juvenile molt period when subadults begin to acquire definitive adult plumage. However, the actual onset of first breeding is deferred even further. The time since birth at first brood was not observed until 1.3 years after hatching [tR = 1.3 years after hatching], again under the standard active body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. The delay between physiological puberty and first reproduction likely reflects the challenges of territory acquisition and pair bond formation in a saturated forest environment. Young birds must locate an appropriate tree cavity and a social partner before initiating their first clutch.

Metabolic measurements provide further insight into the high energetic demands of this active trunk-gleaning insectivore. The basal metabolic rate of a resting adult Dendrocincla merula reaches 112.73 milliliters per hour [JOi = 112.73 milliliters per hour] at a core temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This value, though relatively modest for a passerine of this size, supports a continuous foraging strategy that involves spiraling up coarse-barked tree trunks for arthropods. The same active temperature that characterizes the BMR measurement is maintained across nearly all life-history benchmarks, underscoring the homeothermic stability of the species during the breeding and foraging periods. Comparative work with other woodcreepers suggests that the moderate longevity observed in this genus, which allows multiple breeding opportunities over a lifetime, is partly a function of the regulated metabolic output; slower basal rates may correlate with the extended lifespan relative to similarly sized Neotropical passerines. Future studies should examine how seasonal fluctuations in ambient temperature affect these physiological parameters.
